ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, bc is a horizontal crossbar fixed on the cart, and the block M is strung on the rod, kept stationary relative to the rod by friction. M also suspends a small ball m through a light thin string. At this time the cart is moving to the right with uniformly accelerated motion with acceleration of magnitude a, while M and m are both stationary relative to the cart, and the angle between the thin string and the vertical direction is θ. The acceleration of the cart gradually increases, and M always remains stationary relative to the cart. When the acceleration increases to 2a, ( )
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: The friction force of the crossbar on M increases to 2 times the original

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there is a cart, and inside the cart a horizontal crossbar is fixed, with c and b marked near the two ends of the crossbar. The block M is sleeved on the crossbar; from near M hangs a light thin string, and the lower end of the string is connected to the small ball m. The thin string is inclined toward the lower left relative to the vertical dashed line, and the included angle is marked as θ. Above the cart there is an acceleration arrow a pointing to the right. Then reason: Let the horizontal acceleration of the cart in some comparable relatively stationary state be A. Initially when A=a, the problem statement clearly states that M and m are both stationary relative to the cart; when the acceleration increases to 2a, the problem statement only directly states that M always remains stationary relative to the cart. To use the whole-body method to find a unique multiple, it should be understood according to the quasi-static equilibrium usually implied by the problem: the small ball m is also stationary relative to the cart in the corresponding state and has the same horizontal acceleration A; otherwise, based only on the literal information, the final-state motion of m is undetermined, and the basis for writing equations for the whole body is insufficient. Under the above implicit understanding, regard M and m as one whole. The tension in the thin string is an internal force of the whole and does not affect the force in the horizontal direction on the whole; gravity and other vertical forces also do not provide a horizontal resultant force. The only external horizontal force along the direction of the crossbar is the friction force f of the crossbar on M, so by Newton's second law, f=(M+m)A. Initially A=a, so f_1=(M+m)a; when the acceleration increases to 2a, f_2=(M+m)·2a. Therefore f_2/f_1=2, so the friction force of the crossbar on M becomes 2 times the original.
